sources.title: How To Hit A Basic Tennis Serve with Venus Williams
9 Tips to Serve Like a Pro

good_form: At contact the trunk should be in forward flexion, leaning into the court with the weight transferred forward.
Get the forward-leaning chest through lateral tilt of the trunk, which the speaker says is the main motion in top servers' acceleration, not rotation or extension.
Top servers tilt laterally about 45 degrees in the wind-up; the drill exaggerates this to 50-60 degrees.
Contact at roughly 45 degrees of forward chest lean, from a side angle.
Arm at contact is nearly in line with the shoulders, about 10 degrees of shoulder flexion, with the elbow only slightly above the shoulder line.
Raise the arm only slightly while tilting laterally, rather than lifting it high, so the pec, shoulder and lat can contribute.
At contact the racket sits slightly off to the non-hitting side of the hand (left for a righty, right for a lefty), in a radially deviated wrist position.
Contact is in line with the shoulder and head, toward the inside of the body.
This wrist position lets shoulder internal rotation, forearm pronation and the lat add power.

faults.name: Upright or leaning-back chest at contact
faults.looks_like: Chest is upright or slightly leaning back when the ball is hit, instead of the trunk leaning forward into the court with body weight transferred in.
faults.why_it_matters: Leaning forward gives much more easy force, like pushing on a wall, and also removes tension from the back.
causes: Not transferring body weight forward during acceleration
Not using lateral tilt of the trunk
fixes: Do the wide-stance weight-shift drill: feet stay on the ground, shift weight from back foot to front foot from the wind-up position.
Start with an exaggerated lateral tilt of 50-60 degrees and finish with the back leg flaring out.
After feeling the weight shift, set up into a full serve and focus on the lateral tilt.
Check serve footage for trunk lean at contact.

faults.name: Arm raised too high at contact
faults.looks_like: Chest is more upright and the arm is lifted high, well beyond a near-straight line with the shoulders, instead of tilting laterally and raising the arm slightly.
faults.why_it_matters: With the arm raised past this threshold you can't use the pec, shoulder and lat, so you lose force from the big muscles.
causes: Raising the arm up on acceleration instead of tilting the trunk laterally
Chest being more upright
fixes: Start from the contact checkpoint with the arm in a straight line with the shoulders.
Lift the elbow just slightly, tilt the chest about 45 degrees, and take the racket back with external shoulder rotation so the butt cap points to the back fence.
Toss and swing, getting used to the elbow slightly above the shoulder line while tilting, then build into the full serve.
outcome_effects: Big muscles of the body can't contribute, so less force

faults.name: Racket above the hand at contact
faults.looks_like: The racket is directly above the hand at contact instead of slightly off to the non-hitting side, so the wrist is not radially deviated.
faults.why_it_matters: It stops you from tapping into the maximum power of shoulder internal rotation; racket head speed then comes mainly from wrist flexion.
causes: Not creating the radially deviated contact position
Contact not in line with the shoulder and head
fixes: Practice from inside the court, feeling the radially deviated wrist with the racket face about in line with the shoulder.
Back up gradually, adding external rotation and more force, until you reach the baseline.
Focus on contacting the ball toward the inside of the body.
outcome_effects: Little ball distance in the demo when using internal rotation
Lower power ceiling, since shoulder, forearm pronation and lat contributions are lost

good_form: Keep the ball resting in the fingers, not the palm and not out at the fingertips, for control and a release around eye level.
Keep the tossing arm relaxed so it can drop down to the front thigh at the start of the toss, as many pros do, before lifting.
Treat the toss as a shoulder lift only, with no movement from the elbow or wrist.
Keep the tossing arm straight but loose, not locked out.
In the loaded position the non-dominant (tossing) shoulder is higher than the dominant shoulder.
Keep the tossing arm up during loading, then let it drop as you unload so the dominant arm comes up into contact.
Start the toss as the racket goes back, and bring the ball up as the racket starts to come up.
Practice the toss on its own, then add shadow swings with the racket to time the takeback with the toss.

faults.name: Bending or turning the elbow on the toss
faults.looks_like: The elbow bends or flicks as the ball is tossed up.
faults.why_it_matters: It makes the toss inconsistent, upsets timing and balance, and makes you chase the ball.
causes: Using the elbow to generate extra force on the ball instead of a shoulder lift
fixes: Think of the toss as a shoulder lift only with no elbow movement
Keep the arm straight but loose
Practice the toss in isolation
outcome_effects: Ball flicks back behind the head and is tossed too quickly for the swing
Swing is rushed, out of sync, with bad timing
Ball goes over the head, so you fall off balance and chase the toss

faults.name: Flicking or bending the wrist on the toss
faults.looks_like: The wrist flicks or bends as the ball is released.
faults.why_it_matters: It makes toss placement inconsistent.
causes: A quick wrist flick adds a fast movement to the toss
fixes: Keep the wrist still and lift only from the shoulder
Practice the isolated toss, focusing on only the shoulder lifting
outcome_effects: Toss is too quick for the swing
Ball lands in a different location each time

faults.name: Dropping the tossing arm too quickly
faults.looks_like: The tossing arm drops down fast while the ball is being tossed up.
faults.why_it_matters: The speaker calls it a critical mistake because it affects toss height, timing and rhythm, and loading.
causes: A quick, jerky toss-and-drop motion
fixes: Keep the tossing arm up through the loading position, with the non-dominant shoulder higher than the dominant one
Drop the arm only as you unload, so the dominant arm comes up to contact
outcome_effects: Ball is tossed higher than needed, throwing off timing and rhythm
You collapse into the serve as you approach contact

good_form: Set the back (right) leg back with the heel in position so the trunk and hips are more rotated during toss and wind-up.
Toss with the tossing arm lined up along the baseline, not pointed at the net, for accuracy and fluid placement.
Release the toss at about eye level and let the left arm keep travelling up to point at the sky, slightly away from the body.
Create lateral trunk tilt with the left shoulder higher than the right.
Bend the knees simultaneously as the left arm rises, in a fluid rocking motion.
At the end of the wind-up, keep head, chest and knees in a straight line rather than an arc in the spine, so the leg drive turns into more downward racket-head speed.
Sequence the acceleration as leg drive, then trunk rotation, then the racket edge coming in; this stores elastic energy in the core.
On acceleration, the racket goes down and stays on edge, with the edge pointing down, which creates the pro drop position.
Power the serve from shoulder internal rotation rather than wrist and forearm.
At contact, have the wrist slightly more radially deviated and the next finger slightly higher to get more shoulder internal rotation.
Make contact more in front, with the trunk moving forward into the court on the follow-through.
Finish out to the side with the shoulder internally rotating, not with the arm dropping straight down and around from wrist flexion.

faults.name: Back leg not positioned back enough
faults.looks_like: The back leg sits further up, so the trunk and hip are not rotated enough during toss and wind-up.
faults.why_it_matters: Less rotation gives less power into the serve.
fixes: Position the right leg back with the heel in the right place, as Federer does.
outcome_effects: Less effortless power from the trunk.

faults.name: Toss arm pointing at the net
faults.looks_like: The arm is already pointed toward the net as the toss begins.
faults.why_it_matters: Top servers toss with the arm lined up along the baseline, which gives accuracy and fluidity.
fixes: Start the toss with the arm in line with the baseline.
Release at about eye level and follow through with the arm going straight up at the sky.
outcome_effects: No lateral trunk tilt, so less power.

faults.name: Arc in the spine at the end of the wind-up
faults.looks_like: The line from chest to knees is curved because the spine is kept stable and arched.
faults.why_it_matters: A straight head-to-knee line lets the leg drive turn into more downward racket-head speed and the pro drop.
causes: Naturally wanting to keep the spine stable.
fixes: Finish the wind-up with the head, chest and knees in a straight line.

faults.name: Racket stays open during acceleration
faults.looks_like: The racket face stays open instead of dropping on edge with the edge pointing down.
faults.why_it_matters: With the racket open, power comes only from the wrist and forearm instead of shoulder internal rotation.
causes: Tilting first and then driving the legs, which is the wrong sequence.
fixes: Do controlled shadow swings: drive the legs, then rotate the trunk, then bring the edge in.
Use two rackets and set the tip up on edge. Drive the legs, rotate, and let the weight of the body pull the racket down and around.
Film yourself or use a mirror for feedback.
outcome_effects: Power is limited to the wrist and forearm.

faults.name: Wrong sequencing: tilt before leg drive
faults.looks_like: The player tilts first and then drives the legs.
faults.why_it_matters: Driving the legs and then rotating creates a stretch-shortening cycle that stores elastic energy in the core.
fixes: Practice the order leg drive, then rotation, then the edge going in.
outcome_effects: Less pop and whip in the serve.

faults.name: Wrist not radially deviated at contact
faults.looks_like: The wrist and finger position at contact do not favor shoulder internal rotation.
faults.why_it_matters: Shoulder internal rotation is the number one source of power.
fixes: Put the wrist in a slightly more radially deviated position.
Raise the next finger a little higher.
outcome_effects: Less power from shoulder internal rotation.

faults.name: Trunk going to the side and back after contact
faults.looks_like: The trunk goes to the side and back instead of forward into the court.
faults.why_it_matters: A trunk positioned more in front taps into the momentum going into the shot.
causes: Contact is not made far enough in front.
fixes: Hit variations down the line, and directly down, to force contact further in front.
Pop the ball and finish to the side.
outcome_effects: Less force from momentum going into the shot.

faults.name: Arm dropping straight down on follow-through
faults.looks_like: The arm comes immediately down and around after the swing, powered by the wrist flexing down.
faults.why_it_matters: The wrist is a much smaller muscle than the shoulder, so it produces less power.
causes: Powering the serve with the wrist rather than shoulder internal rotation.
fixes: Do smooth serves that emphasize contact and finish, feeling shoulder internal rotation.
Hit straight down the line to force the shoulder to rotate internally and finish out to the side.

good_form: Use a continental grip: base knuckle of the index finger and heel pad on bevel two.
Start with the racket face slightly open, strings angled slightly up (to the left for a righty), which encourages the continental grip.
Toss first, then bend the knees; the bend happens as the racket rises toward the top of the head.
Explode up as the racket drops behind you.
Bring the racket up on its edge, like knocking off a birthday hat, and deliberately hit side spin.
Swing in the direction opposite to the way you want the ball to curve, not toward the target.
Even flat serves should carry some side spin, just less of it.
Pronate on every serve (flat, kick, slice), whatever the direction.
Pronation is palm toward you turning to palm away, thumb down; it is the fastest way to move the hand.
Contact the ball before the racket is square, about 85 degrees on a 0-to-180 path, with the right edge (for a righty) slightly in front.
After contact the racket squares up and keeps turning so the strings face right (for a righty); don't brake the pronation.
Bending the elbow, as Sampras does, can help pronation for less flexible players.
Finish with a power X: pull the tossing arm in against the body, like hugging yourself, to speed up the hitting arm.
From behind, the tossing hand should wave to the camera on the hitting side.
Sequence: toss and reach toward the opponent, then wave to the camera.

faults.name: Forehand grip on serve
faults.looks_like: Using a forehand grip; starting the serve with strings pointing down or bouncing the ball on the racket face.
faults.why_it_matters: It has a very low ceiling and limits how good the serve can get; pros don't use it for their best serves. It also prevents learning side-spin serves.
causes: Habit of using a forehand grip, which lets you learn to serve quickly
fixes: Switch to a continental grip.
Start with the racket face slightly open, strings angled slightly up (left for a righty).
Film yourself to check.
outcome_effects: Fast first serve, but a ball slightly out forces a weak tapped second serve
Cannot curve the ball with side spin; the ball goes flat into its back

faults.name: Bending knees before the toss
faults.looks_like: Bending the knees first, then tossing the ball.
faults.why_it_matters: The knee bend then gives no benefit. Getting the timing right can greatly increase racket speed, which can go into spin and pace.
causes: Not realizing the timing is wrong, even among long-time players
fixes: Toss first, then bend.
Time the bend as the racket rises toward the head, then explode up as the racket drops behind.
Film yourself to check.
outcome_effects: Can't explode up as the racket drops behind you

faults.name: Waiter's tray (strings facing sky, flat serve mentality)
faults.looks_like: Strings face the sky as the racket comes up, so they then face forward, aiming to smack the back of the ball.
faults.why_it_matters: It stops you learning to bring the racket up on edge and hit side spin.
causes: Mentality of hitting only flat serves, or no particular serve type
Swinging toward the target as with a forehand grip
fixes: Bring the racket around on its edge, leading up with the edge.
Deliberately hit side spin, swinging opposite to the desired curve.
Don't swing toward the target.
Keep some side spin even on flat serves.
outcome_effects: Ball goes flat with no spin
When first practicing side spin, swinging toward the target sends the ball way off to the side

faults.name: No pronation / supinating around the ball
faults.looks_like: Going palm up then palm down, carving around the ball; or pronating a little, then supinating; or hitting and finishing with strings still facing left (righty).
faults.why_it_matters: Pronation is the fastest hand move and gives racket speed; speaker says pros do not curl and supinate around the ball.
causes: Believing you must go around the ball to hit slice
Confusion that contact on the edge side can't make the ball curve the other way
Braking the forearm turn after contact
fixes: Pronate on every serve.
Contact at about 85 degrees with the right edge slightly in front (righty).
Keep rotating after contact so strings face right (righty).
Stay loose and let momentum carry the follow-through.
Bend the elbow if less flexible.
outcome_effects: Less racket speed and less control from spin
Slice does not come from going around the ball

faults.name: Throwing the tossing arm back
faults.looks_like: Tossing arm swung back behind the body and held out, rotating the body as you hit and holding balance.
faults.why_it_matters: Pulling the tossing arm in stops the body and accelerates the hitting arm, like a whip cracking; rotating through contact is not in your best interest. Serves can still be good but not your best.
causes: Coaches teaching it
It looks cool, and juniors like the look
Belief that it is about balance
fixes: Finish with a power X, hugging yourself with arms crossed.
Keep the tossing arm in against the body like Nadal.
Film from behind: the tossing hand should wave to the camera on the hitting side.
Toss, reach toward the opponent, then wave to the camera.
outcome_effects: Less hitting-arm acceleration and racket speed

good_form: You hit the serve ball with the forearm via pronation; the shoulder is a link in the kinetic chain but not the last link.
From the backstretch the racket keeps flicking out and away (forearm supinating) rather than going up toward the ball, until max forearm stretch, then flicks in and up.
Max forearm stretch comes after the back scratch position; the back scratch is just a random position the forearm passes through.
Max shoulder stretch is near the back scratch, but forearm stays stretched even as the shoulder rotates forward.
Think of scratching a partner's back (max forearm stretch) rather than your own back (max shoulder stretch).
Throw the shoulder to load and fire the forearm, perceiving the forearm action.
Strong servers like Alcaraz, Sampras and Sabalenka show a big supinated forearm stretch followed by an explosive pronation in a split second.
Imagine the racket smacking through the ball and stay aware of late links in the chain, such as the forearm.
Drill: practise forearm rotation (pronation/supination) in front of you with minimal shoulder, then with the racket above your head, repeating stretch-fire.
Drill: toss the ball so it would land on your head and bop it with the forearm, stretching out then in, hitting to the baseline rather than into the box at first.
Visualise an out-to-in, horizontal racket action with the tip on the inside of the hand, though the actual racket will be about 45 degrees up.
Let the forearm roll out, in, out, in, with the shoulder rolling only enough to let the forearm stretch and bop.

faults.name: Back scratch glitch (jackknifing racket up to the ball)
faults.looks_like: From the back scratch position the player goes straight up and over the top, jackknifing the racket to the ball with little outward drift or forearm stretch.
faults.why_it_matters: The forearm doesn't get stretched into supination, so the player loses the explosive pronation and the whack that comes from the forearm; the speaker links it to weaker servers.
causes: Not realising the ball is hit with the forearm
Focusing on the shoulder and its max stretch as the key position
Brain thinking the ball must be hit a different way than it actually is
fixes: Learn to feel the forearm as the last link in the chain
Practise forearm rotation drills without a ball, in front of you then above your head
Bop tossed balls with the forearm, tossing to land on your head
Think of the back scratch as a random position the forearm passes through and let the racket roll out, then in
outcome_effects: Serve gets stuck at the back scratch position

good_form: Make a good first move by turning the shoulders at the start.
Use a true continental grip.
Keep the racket face closed (with the continental grip) as the racket comes up.
Get the elbow up into the trophy position, 'elbowing the enemy'.
Think of the motion like throwing a football or baseball, with the elbow up and never tucked down.
Let the racket drop fully behind rather than only partway.
The swing should flow effortlessly, not like a catapult.

faults.name: Low elbow / tucking the elbow
faults.looks_like: Shoulders turn well at first, but as the racket comes up the elbow tucks down and in, then the player flips up and serves from that position without a proper trophy position.
faults.why_it_matters: It puts a lot of stress on the arm and can contribute to elbow and shoulder problems. It also costs power and consistency, and the swing becomes a effortful catapult instead of flowing.
causes: Racket face opens and the player pushes at the ball
Forehand-leaning grip instead of a true continental
Starting from a full swing, so the arms move at the wrong pace and in the wrong way
Technical inefficiency or not understanding the swing
Body limitations such as a hip issue or shoulder limitation causing compensations
fixes: Use a true continental grip
Start from a three-quarter serve, bend the elbow and turn the shoulders
If that fails, start from a half motion or with the racket and elbow already up, and don't let the elbow drop
Pretend to throw a football or baseball
Serve into a side fence or curtain while exaggerating a very high elbow, without worrying about the result
Practice finding the trophy position with eyes closed for body awareness
Do corrective exercises for body limitations

faults.name: Forehand grip with racket face flipping open
faults.looks_like: The racket flips open as it comes up, and the player pushes at the ball with a forehand-style grip.
faults.why_it_matters: It makes the trophy position difficult and leads to the low elbow and a push swing.
causes: Grip is not a true continental and is closer to a forehand grip
fixes: Use a true continental grip
Keep the racket face closed as it comes up
outcome_effects: Poor racket drop, with the racket dropping only partway

good_form: Use a continental (chopper) grip, which gives the most snap, allows pronation and lets you hit into the shot.
Keep a little space between the index finger and the rest of the hand rather than gripping in a fist; this gives a slight angle, helps you reach higher and lets the grip rotate easily.
Stand sideways to the court with the left shoulder toward the opponent.
Make contact nice and high above the shoulder.
Toss slightly above where the racket reaches, so the ball is just beginning to drop when you hit it; the speaker thinks of about one racket length above the racket head for a classic serve.
Keep the toss in front of you and straight, with a down-then-up rhythm; practise tossing and catching without moving much and without the ball spinning.
Time the leg bend with the toss: bend as the ball leaves the hand, then drive up.

Set a tilted shoulder line with the left shoulder up and the right dropped (trophy pose), then replace the left shoulder with the right like a seesaw to generate power with shoulder tilt, rotation and leg drive.
Match toss timing to your natural rhythm: the abbreviated serve is fast-slow-fast with a slightly lower toss, and the classic serve is slow-fast, slow-fast with more time.
Have the arm up and shoulders tilted as the ball reaches its apex.
To find a player's natural rhythm, watch how they throw a ball, ideally a heavier one such as an American football, which is harder to cheat with.

faults.name: Frying-pan (semi-western) grip
faults.looks_like: Starting the serve with a semi-western, frying-pan style grip instead of a continental grip.
faults.why_it_matters: The player cannot generate power or snap, or get the accuracy needed on the serve.
fixes: Move the grip around toward the continental/chopper grip, even though it feels strange at first.
Stand sideways and make contact high above the shoulder so the grip can turn and relax.
outcome_effects: No snap from the top to let the ball come down

faults.name: Contact too low with continental grip
faults.looks_like: Meeting the ball low, so the strings cannot open up and the racket slices the right side of the ball.
faults.why_it_matters: Contact feels inconsistent and the ball gets sliced.
causes: Contact point is too low
fixes: Stand sideways with the left shoulder toward the opponent.
Toss so contact is nice and high above the shoulder.
outcome_effects: Ball is sliced off the right side

faults.name: Gripping the racket like a fist
faults.looks_like: Holding the chopper grip as a closed fist with no space between the index finger and the rest of the hand.
faults.why_it_matters: It limits reach and easy grip rotation, and so limits easy power.
fixes: Leave a little space between the index finger and the rest of the hand to create a slight angle.

faults.name: Toss too low
faults.looks_like: Contact is made low with the strings facing down.
faults.why_it_matters: It is harder to open the racket face into contact.
causes: Toss is too low relative to the racket's reach
fixes: Toss slightly above the racket so the ball begins to drop as you hit it, about one racket length above the racket head for the classic serve.

faults.name: Toss too high
faults.looks_like: After the ball leaves the hand you stay crouched with bent legs for too long, waiting for the ball to come down.
faults.why_it_matters: Timing becomes harder and the motion stops being dynamic, with muscles losing energy; it is also harder in sun and wind.
causes: The ball goes up too high, so you wait in the leg bend
Ball drops faster into the racket from a higher toss
fixes: Time the leg bend with the toss.
Use a slightly lower toss, as in the abbreviated serve.
Practise a down-then-up rhythm.
outcome_effects: Loss of dynamic energy into contact

faults.name: Forcing the wrong serve rhythm
faults.looks_like: Teaching or using an abbreviated serve when the player's natural throwing rhythm is the slower classic one (or the reverse).
faults.why_it_matters: It goes against the player's natural predisposition.
causes: Not checking the player's natural throwing motion first
fixes: Watch how the player throws a ball, using a heavier ball if needed, and build the serve around that rhythm.

good_form: Reach the trophy position before the power position: racket back, elbow bent, racket tip pointing up to the sky.
In the trophy position the wrist bends slightly toward the little finger (ulnar deviation, like a royal wave), setting up a later move toward the thumb.
The racket drops into the power position (tip pointing at the ground, racket behind the back) only after the shoulders start rotating and the elbow begins to rise.
That racket flip creates racket head lag, so the racket whips through and catches up with the hand at contact for racket head speed.
Lift the racket arm more slowly than the ball toss arm, disconnecting the two arms so the racket stays tall in the trophy position.
Start the toss arm low and lift it gradually for better timing and a consistent toss height.

faults.name: Reaching the power position too early
faults.looks_like: The racket collapses and drops behind the back (tip pointing at the ground) before the shoulders rotate and the elbow rises, skipping through the trophy position.
faults.why_it_matters: It is one of the biggest differences between top ATP players and club players, and can cut potential racket speed in half.
causes: Racket arm moving too fast or collapsing, not staying tall in the trophy position
Rushed, quick or jerky ball toss that makes the racket arm speed up too, since the arms naturally move together
fixes: Lift the racket arm slower than the toss arm to disconnect the two arms, so the racket stands tall in the trophy position (it may feel awkward like tapping head and rubbing stomach)
Start the toss arm lower and lift it more gradually
Drill: put a tennis ball in a sock and swing it like a serve to feel the flow, shoulder turn and rhythm

good_form: Use a circular racket motion on the serve rather than pushing the ball into the box.
After the toss, lift the racket to about chest height with the palm down and strings pointing down, so a ball could sit in the throat of the racket.
Salute: with the palm down, bring the racket up with the strings pointing down the whole way.
The racket should pass in over the head, as Osaka, Federer, Kyrgios, Djokovic and Groth do.
Practise the salute with a ball in the racket throat, keeping it from falling out. The speaker says Federer's racket does not stay this way, but he still hits the hat every time.
Wear a birthday hat on the front of the head like a unicorn horn and hit it with the racket on the serve. It gives instant feedback on whether the racket moves in over the head.

faults.name: Waiter's tray serve
faults.looks_like: As soon as the ball is tossed, the racket opens up with the palm and strings pointing to the sky, and the player pushes the ball into the box.
faults.why_it_matters: The speaker calls it a killer for many players. It is the opposite of the proper circular service motion, and he says it is very hard to serve this way.
causes: Opening the racket right after the toss, with the palm and strings turned up to the sky
fixes: Drill 1: toss, lift the racket to chest height and freeze with the palm and strings down, so a ball could sit in the throat.
Drill 2: salute with the strings pointing down the whole time, optionally with a ball in the racket throat that never falls out.
Drill 3: wear a birthday hat on the front of the head and hit it with the racket when serving.
Do the shadow swings anywhere, even at home.
outcome_effects: The ball is pushed into the box rather than hit with a circular motion.
The racket misses the birthday hat, which shows the racket is not passing in over the head.

faults.name: Birthday hat placed at the back of the head
faults.looks_like: The birthday hat sits on the back of the head instead of the front.
faults.why_it_matters: The speaker says this is why some coaches wrongly criticise the birthday hat drill.
causes: Putting the hat in the wrong spot
fixes: Place the hat on the front part of the head like a unicorn horn.
outcome_effects: The hat no longer separates a waiter's tray swing from the correct motion, because a waiter's tray swing would not hit it at the front.

good_form: Stand about one step from the middle mark when serving to the deuce side and about two steps away for the ad side, to keep a good angle.
Point the front foot's toe at the net post, roughly 45° to the baseline, with the back foot following that line and staying on the correct side of it.
Keep the back foot parallel to the baseline for balance and the ability to push up; the setup is the same on both sides.
Line the tossing arm up along the net-post line so it points the same direction.
Use a continental (hammer-like) grip, with a slight gap between the index finger and the other fingers so the hand stays relaxed and can reach higher.
Beginners can start from an eastern forehand grip, which makes pronation and showing the strings to the ball easier, and move toward continental later.
Treat the toss as placing the ball, not throwing it: keep the arm straight from the shoulder, hold the ball in the fingertips, and open the fingers to release with a still wrist.
A good toss has little spin and rises still, as if placed on a platform at the top; it should be neither too high nor too low.
Hit serves from high to low, except for kick serves.
Reach a trophy position with the tossing arm pointing up, an L shape in the arm, and the tossing shoulder above the hitting shoulder; this brings in the obliques and hips.
Toss with the arm only, without dipping the legs for the toss; start on the back foot and move forward as the arm goes down then up.
Timing runs back foot to front foot; bend the legs as the ball rises and straighten up to reach it as it drops.
Let the racket loop behind like two relaxed pendulums, with the elbow rising to contact as the racket drops, to build racket-head speed.
Keep the swing moving without stopping or pausing, and keep the arm loose.
If you struggle to sync the arms, start with the racket already up in the trophy position and think only about dropping and hitting.
The abbreviated serve skips the bottom of the pendulum and goes straight up; it is compact and gives a lot of wrist snap and power.
At contact, aim for a flat racket face toward the target, especially as a beginner, using pronation (opening the wrist from a supinated position).
Contact high, in front and slightly to the side so the wrist can pronate.

faults.name: Back foot breaks the net-post line
faults.looks_like: The back foot ends up on the wrong side of the line to the net post, so the stance is too open before the serve.
faults.why_it_matters: You want to be sideways for a good wind-up, so an open stance spoils that.
fixes: Draw an imaginary line to the net post and keep the back foot on the correct side of it, never crossing it.
Point the front toe at the net post and keep the back foot in line with it.
outcome_effects: Too open before the serve, with less wind-up

faults.name: Foot faulting over the middle line
faults.looks_like: With a wide stance, the heel ends up over the middle line.
faults.why_it_matters: It is a foot fault.
causes: Stepping back too wide in the setup
fixes: If your stance is wide, position yourself further to the right so the heel stays off the middle line.

faults.name: Tight fist grip
faults.looks_like: The hand is clenched tight with no space between the index finger and the other fingers.
faults.why_it_matters: It is hard to release and relax, and it limits reach.
fixes: Leave a small space between the index finger and the rest of the hand, holding the racket like a hammer with a slight angle.

faults.name: Chopping or slicing at the ball
faults.looks_like: With a continental grip, the racket goes at the ball with a chopping motion and only the top of the strings opens to it.
faults.why_it_matters: You cannot make good contact or show the full strings to the ball.
causes: Lack of wrist pronation or rotation
Toss too low, so the wrist cannot pronate
Contact not high enough in front and to the side
fixes: Toss higher and make contact high, in front and slightly to the side.
Show the strings to the ball.
Beginners can use an eastern forehand grip temporarily to feel pronation.
Keep a small gap between the index finger and the hand.

faults.name: Toss too high or too low
faults.looks_like: The ball is placed outside the optimal height for reaching up and hitting on the stretch.
faults.why_it_matters: You need to hit from high to low at full stretch.
fixes: Think of the toss as placing the ball at the optimal height.
outcome_effects: Slicing if the toss is too low

faults.name: Flicked, gripped toss
faults.looks_like: The ball is held tight in the palm or flicked with the wrist, and spins a lot in the air.
faults.why_it_matters: The toss goes everywhere, so you cannot serve consistently.
causes: Gripping the ball too tight in the palm
Flicking the wrist on release
fixes: Hold the ball in the fingers, not the palm.
Keep the arm straight and the hand still, and just open the fingers.
Check the toss: the ball should barely spin.

faults.name: Using the legs to toss and tossing from a dead stop
faults.looks_like: Dipping the legs and rising to toss, or already being forward on the front foot when tossing; or holding the tossing hand still before tossing.
faults.why_it_matters: The ball is light and needs no legs, and the timing is lost.
fixes: Toss with the arm only.
Start on the back foot, with the front toe up, and move forward as the arm drops down then up.
Use down-then-up arm motion for a consistent toss.
outcome_effects: Nowhere left to go in the motion

faults.name: Tight, stopped swing with no loop
faults.looks_like: The racket goes down very tightly, or pauses or stops at the bottom or top of the swing.
faults.why_it_matters: The racket loses momentum and speed that the shot needs.
causes: Manufacturing the loop
Stiff, tense arm
fixes: Keep the arm relaxed like a pendulum and let the loop happen naturally.
Keep the motion continuous, slowing but never stopping.
Let the strings carry the speed to contact.

faults.name: Abbreviated serve with shoulder problems
faults.looks_like: Using the short, compact abbreviated serve motion.
faults.why_it_matters: It may not suit players with shoulder issues; the full motion is more relaxed and forgiving on the arm.
fixes: Learn the full, relaxed motion instead if you have shoulder problems.

good_form: Use an eastern grip for the serve, with the thumb knuckle on the left bevel, rather than the western forehand grip.
Keep the index finger spread slightly up the handle, not a fist, so the wrist can move and direct the ball.
Racket should be on edge with the wrist cocked at the set position, not flat like a pancake.
Hold the ball in the fingertips like an ice cream cone, not squeezed in the palm.
Keep the tossing arm straight and simply release the ball straight up so it lands in the same spot every time.
Beginners: point the front foot toward the net post, bend the knees and explode up without stepping.
If stepping, don't step past the toes, and start with the back foot directly behind the front foot.
Keep the shoulders closed as long as possible; the shoulder turn gives power, disguise and control.
Get the hitting arm quickly into a roughly 90-degree, parallel-to-ground position with the racket on edge and wrist cocked; film yourself to check.
Aim with the hand and wrist toward the target, and contact different sides of the ball (about three o'clock for a wide serve in the deuce court).
Toss high enough to hit at full arm extension at the apex, but not so high you wait for the ball.
Hit up on the ball first, then snap the wrist to bring it down.
Keep shoulders and chest up during the snap; only the wrist snaps.
Finish by tucking the arm, keeping shoulders up and landing inside the court past the baseline, then recover ready for the return.

faults.name: Western grip on serve
faults.looks_like: Using the comfortable forehand western grip so the racket and wrist are flat like a frying pan.
faults.why_it_matters: Racket can't be on edge with the wrist cocked, so you can't direct the ball or make spin to control it into the box.
causes: The western grip feels comfortable because it's the forehand grip, and newbies keep the habit
fixes: Switch to an eastern grip with thumb knuckle on the left bevel
Move the index finger up a little so it isn't a fist and the wrist can work
outcome_effects: Serve is harder to control and get in the box

faults.name: Gripping the ball too tightly
faults.looks_like: Squeezing the ball in the palm with a death grip.
faults.why_it_matters: A tight hold hurts a clean release and the consistent toss.
causes: Holding the ball in the palm and squeezing
fixes: Hold the ball like an ice cream cone in the fingertips, without squeezing

faults.name: Bending the tossing arm
faults.looks_like: Bending the arm while tossing the ball.
faults.why_it_matters: The toss must be in the same place every time, or you chase the ball and can't serve.
causes: Bending the arm during the toss instead of keeping it straight
fixes: Keep the arm straight, hold the ball on the fingertips and just release as the arm goes straight up

faults.name: Stepping past the toes / misplaced back foot
faults.looks_like: Stepping out beyond the toes, or starting with the back foot out to the side or far from the front foot.
faults.why_it_matters: Footwork needs to be correct because every step matters.
fixes: Step only up to the toes, not past them
Start the back foot right behind the front foot, then step

faults.name: Opening the shoulders too soon
faults.looks_like: Shoulders turn open early instead of staying closed.
faults.why_it_matters: You lose the power from the upper-body turn and the disguise, and you lose control of the ball.
fixes: Start with shoulders closed and keep them closed as long as possible
outcome_effects: Wild serves flying all over the place

faults.name: Arm too low in the set position
faults.looks_like: Hitting arm is down low rather than at about 90 degrees, parallel to the ground, with racket on edge and wrist cocked.
faults.why_it_matters: The correct position gives consistency and sets up advanced serves like the kick serve.
fixes: Put the arm immediately into the 90-degree position with racket on edge and wrist cocked
Film yourself to check and track progress

faults.name: Toss too high causing a hitch
faults.looks_like: Waiting on the ball to come down, with a pause in the motion.
faults.why_it_matters: It breaks down the serve under pressure; the motion should be continuous.
causes: Tossing so high that you wait for the ball
fixes: Toss to where the arm is fully extended and hit the ball at its apex
Keep the service motion continuous

faults.name: Toss too low / arm not extended
faults.looks_like: Motion too short so the arm isn't fully extended at contact.
faults.why_it_matters: The arm needs to be extended at contact.
causes: Toss too short
fixes: Toss high enough for full arm extension

faults.name: Dropping the body or shoulders on the wrist snap
faults.looks_like: Bending or bowing the body down and letting the shoulders drop as you snap.
faults.why_it_matters: You should stay tall and confident, snapping only with the wrist.
causes: Bringing the body down along with the wrist snap
fixes: Hit up first then snap with only the wrist
Keep shoulders and chest up

faults.name: Not recovering after the serve
faults.looks_like: Standing and admiring the serve instead of getting back.
faults.why_it_matters: The ball comes back, possibly right at you, and you must be ready.
fixes: Land inside the court clearing the baseline, then recover immediately

good_form: Serving is like throwing: the front shoulder points toward the target and aims with the arm, then the other shoulder takes its place.
Keep the arm and hand completely loose and free so the racket head accelerates like a throw.
Use a two-part rhythm: first load and take energy, then accelerate when it feels right; it is one continuous motion in two beats.
Push in the intended direction rather than just pushing upward.
Once in position, lead with the hand/arm first and let the legs follow, without thinking about the legs.
For a slice serve, hit the ball on its side and stay under it.
Toss the ball to the right so that at contact it is further right; it should cross the line on the right before the racket reaches it, which makes slicing easier.
Hit the slice close to the net; the goal is to hear a crisp sound, which comes from a completely free arm and is where the acceleration comes from.

faults.name: Going over the top of the ball on a slice
faults.looks_like: The racket passes over the top of the ball instead of staying under and hitting the side.
faults.why_it_matters: You can't slice the ball once you pass over it; passing over is fine only for kick or flat serves.
fixes: Stay under the ball and hit it on its side.
Exaggerate hitting the side of the ball.

faults.name: Contacting the ball too far toward the middle/left
faults.looks_like: Hitting the ball in a position closer to the front or center rather than on its side, with the toss not far enough right.
faults.why_it_matters: Contact on the side gives height over the net and a ball that is hard to return; otherwise there is less sidespin and it is easier to return.
causes: Toss not placed far enough to the right
fixes: Keep the toss on the right so the ball crosses the right line before the slice.
Hit the ball on its side.
outcome_effects: Ball more likely to hit the net

faults.name: Tight, restricted arm
faults.looks_like: The arm and racket are not completely free during acceleration.
faults.why_it_matters: Acceleration comes from a free arm, and the crisp sound of contact depends on it.
fixes: Feel the arm completely free, as when throwing the racket head.

faults.name: Leading with legs instead of the hand
faults.looks_like: Thinking about pushing with the legs first rather than going with the hand.
faults.why_it_matters: Sequence should start with the hand/arm, with the legs following.
fixes: Think only about going with the hand first, and let the legs follow.
